channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: TrustMH-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating the Trustworthiness of Large Language Models in Mental Health, arXiv, 2026
item.description: A team at Renmin University maps mental health specific norms onto eight measurable pillars, reliability, crisis identification and escalation, safety, fairness, privacy, robustness, anti sycophancy, and ethics, then runs six general purpose and six specialized mental health models through all of them. Every model underperforms somewhere, and even generally powerful systems fail to hold high performance across all dimensions at once, which is the specific claim vendors tend to make.

item.title: EMPATH: A Multilingual Auditor Judge Benchmark for Safety Evaluation of Emotional Support Chatbots, arXiv, 2026
item.description: Introduces a benchmark that pairs an auditor model with a judge model to probe the safety of emotional support chatbots, structured so failures can be attributed to specific interaction turns rather than averaged into a single score. The multilingual design is the part worth watching, since guardrails tuned on English routinely thin out in other languages, which matters most where clinical services are least available.

item.title: Illusions of Intelligence, Connection and Reality: Perils of Large Language AI Models for People with Severe Mental Illness, Australasian Psychiatry, 2026
item.description: Looi and colleagues write specifically about people whose reality testing is impaired by psychosis, severe depression, or bipolar disorder, a group usually handled as an edge case in general chatbot safety work. Their argument is that fluent, agreeable systems supply an illusion of intelligence and connection to precisely the users least equipped to discount it, and they connect that dynamic to self harm risk rather than treating it as a matter of user preference.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Psychiatry: Clinical Applications, Limitations, and Ethical Challenges, Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, 2026
item.description: Pedro Morgado argues that headline accuracy figures in psychiatric AI come from internally validated research settings, that external validation remains rare, and that evidence of real world clinical impact is scarce, all while sensitive mental health data concentrates in the hands of large technology companies. The sharpest point is methodological: defining normality from statistical distributions installs a culturally contingent concept as a medical standard, with direct consequences for the pathologization of human diversity.

item.title: Disclosure Is Not Destigmatization: Rethinking AI and Mental Health Stigma, Frontiers in Public Health, 2026
item.description: Separates stigma reduction from stigma buffering: people disclose more to chatbots because the interpersonal cost of disclosing is lower, not because stigmatizing attitudes have shifted in families, workplaces, or clinics. Willingness to talk to a machine is therefore a poor proxy for progress, and the authors note that language models have themselves produced stigmatizing responses toward conditions including borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders.

item.title: A11y-CUA Dataset: Characterizing the Accessibility Gap in Computer Use Agents, arXiv, 2026
item.description: Computer use agents operate interfaces by pointing, clicking, and typing, which mirrors how sighted users work and lets those users watch the agent and take back control mid task. Blind and low vision users who rely on assistive technology have no equivalent handle, so the authors build a dataset characterizing exactly where that shared control breaks down instead of treating accessibility as something to patch afterward.

item.title: Beyond Her: Safety Dynamics in Role Play AI Companions, arXiv, 2026
item.description: Looks at how safety behaves inside role play companion systems, where the product incentive to stay in character pulls directly against refusing, redirecting, or breaking frame on a harmful exchange. Companion apps are the same category named in reports of emotional dependence and delusion reinforcement, which makes persona persistence a safety property rather than a styling decision.

item.title: People First Chatbot Act Would Require Monthly Chatbot Safety Assessments, H.R. 9619, July 2026
item.description: Introduced by Reps. Foushee and Casar, the bill would require chatbot providers to run monthly safety assessments for suicide, emotional dependence, and compulsive usage, bar providers from implying that outputs are equivalent to advice from licensed healthcare, legal, or financial professionals, and prohibit training on minors chat logs. Enforcement runs through the FTC, state attorneys general, and a private right of action, the provision that lets harmed users act without waiting on regulator capacity.
